    Each year, we at ESPN Fantasy endeavor to help with your fantasy football draft prep, including sleepers lists and cheat sheets. Below, you will get the best of both worlds, as ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter offers up his personal list of early-, middle- and late-rounds targets in 2026 fantasy drafts.

    Below are some players who are poised to be fantasy standouts this season. Obviously, they aren't the only ones with a chance to excel, but this is a distinguishing part: These are some of the players who have a real chance to outperform their current average draft position (ADP). If given a choice at certain junctures in the draft, or in tiebreaker situations, these are players who will receive strong consideration.

    In this space last season, one of the recommended middle-rounds values was wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and some of the later-rounds values included quarterbacks Drake Maye and Trevor Lawrence, wide receiver Emeka Egbuka, and running back Quinshon Judkins.

    I am in one 12-team league, in which some of these players will not need to be drafted, and one 16-team league, in which some of them might be more valuable. But again, these players hold strong value relative to their ESPN ADPs and are in a position to have productive seasons.

    I hope this list is helpful. Good luck this season.

    NOTE: For the purposes of this column, the round ranges listed are based on ADP relative to 10-team leagues: "early" refers to Rounds 1-4, "middle" to Rounds 5-11 and "later" to Rounds 12 or higher.

    Quarterback

    There's nothing wrong with drafting a quarterback such as Josh Allen or Lamar Jackson early. But there is so much depth at the position this year that there can be strong values found in the middle-to-late rounds. This is why you'll see no QBs listed as early-rounds targets below.

    Middle rounds

    Bo Nix, Broncos (ADP: 86.3): Nix's ability to rack up fantasy points with his legs as much as his arm is underappreciated.

    Caleb Williams, Bears (ADP: 92.2): His talent was on full display last season and, after a year in Ben Johnson's offense, he should be even more improved.

    Justin Herbert, Chargers (ADP: 106.0): Matched with Mike McDaniel as his offensive coordinator, Herbert could be in line for his best NFL season.

    Later rounds

    Tyler Shough, Saints (ADP: 155.4): He flashed as a rookie last season and is expected to make continued growth in Year 2.

    Jordan Love, Packers (ADP: 158.0): Team officials are confident he's set up to take the next step this season.

    Daniel Jones, Colts (ADP: 158.2): Jones was one of the best fantasy QBs last season until he was injured -- and now he looks to be healthy.

    Running back

    A case can be made to draft Bijan Robinson or Jahmyr Gibbs with the No. 1 pick in fantasy football this season. There is talent sprinkled across the position, including some intriguing late-rounds picks.

    Early rounds

    Jahmyr Gibbs, Lions (ADP: 1.4): He might be the most dangerous offensive threat in the NFL, one with 38 touchdowns in the past two seasons.

    Bijan Robinson, Falcons (ADP: 2.5): Robinson and Gibbs will -- and should -- be going 1-2 in almost every fantasy football draft.

    Chase Brown, Bengals (ADP: 21.9): He is the lead back and a multipurpose threat in one of the highest-scoring offenses in the NFL.

    Kenneth Walker III, Chiefs (ADP: 22.3): He has never finished higher than RB18 in a fantasy season, but he seems set to shatter that mark in 2026.

    Omarion Hampton, Chargers (ADP: 25.3): When healthy last season, he was highly productive. If he's healthy this season, he will be again.

    Middle rounds

    Bhayshul Tuten, Jaguars (ADP: 71.8): The Jaguars loved him coming out of college, and that hasn't changed heading into his second season.

    Rhamondre Stevenson, Patriots (ADP: 83.1): Always overlooked, always productive.

    Later rounds

    Kenny Gainwell, Buccaneers (ADP: 116.5): Bucs have raved about the different skills he brings to the offense.

    Blake Corum, Rams (ADP: 135.1): He will share work with Kyren Williams ... and be drafted many rounds later.

    Jordan Mason, Vikings (ADP: 138.9): The Vikings seem determined to get their run game going, and Mason will benefit.

    Chris Rodriguez Jr., Jaguars (ADP: 165.6): Head coach Liam Coen has been a fan of Rodriguez since they worked together at Kentucky.

    Jonah Coleman, Broncos (ADP: 169.4): Denver's backfield is crowded, but some have compared Coleman to Maurice Jones-Drew.

    MarShawn Lloyd, Packers (ADP: 170.1): Lloyd has never been healthy at the NFL level but was healthy this summer.

    Wide receiver

    At a time when the league is passing more than ever, there are receivers in every tier who can help fantasy teams.

    Early rounds

    Ja'Marr Chase, Bengals (ADP: 4.0): Chase has lofty touchdown goals for the season and the talent to match.

    Puka Nacua, Rams (ADP: 5.2): He still has plenty on the line as he heads into the final year of his contract.

    Justin Jefferson, Vikings (ADP: 12.1): As talented as any receiver in the league and poised for a bounce-back season.

    Chris Olave, Saints (ADP: 31.1): He is expected to be the team's leading receiver in a high-paced offense.

    Middle rounds

    DeVonta Smith, Eagles (ADP: 40.4): Minus A.J. Brown, there should be even more targets for the talented and tough Smith.

    Ladd McConkey, Chargers (ADP: 50.1): With Mike McDaniel as his offensive coordinator, McConkey could become the focal point of the Chargers' passing attack.

    Luther Burden III, Bears (ADP: 76.2): Head coach Ben Johnson has compared Burden to Amon-Ra St. Brown.

    Parker Washington, Jaguars (ADP: 93.3): Washington's talents shined at the end of last season and again in training camp.

    Later rounds

    Wan'Dale Robinson, Titans (ADP: 113.4): Former Giants head coach and current Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll fed him the football in New York last season, and now he gets to do the same in Tennessee.

    Jordan Addison, Vikings (ADP: 114.1): With Kyler Murray at quarterback, Addison should make many plays downfield.

    Josh Downs, Colts (ADP: 136.6): The older brother of Cowboys rookie safety Caleb Downs. This Downs is set to make his own mark.

    KC Concepcion, Browns (ADP: 144.1): Even as a rookie, he's expected to have a prominent role in the Browns' offense.

    Ja'Kobi Lane, Ravens (ADP: 167.7): A third-round pick this past spring, Lane was the star of Baltimore's training camp.

    Caleb Douglas, Dolphins (ADP: 169.4): Everybody struggled to cover him at a recent practice against the Commanders.

    Cyrus Allen, Chiefs (ADP: 169.5): One of the most talked about players at Chiefs camp this summer.

    Kayshon Boutte, Texans (ADP: 170.7): The talent has always been there, and now he has the opportunity to be the WR2 in Houston.

    Pat Bryant, Broncos (ADP: 170.6): Bryant looks ready to shine in his second season.

    Ryan Flournoy, Cowboys (ADP: 170.9): CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens aren't the only Cowboys receivers who will produce this season.

    Tre' Harris, Chargers (ADP: 171.0): Like Bryant, he is poised to make a jump in his second season.

    Devaughn Vele, Saints (ADP: 171.5): Showed a connection with Shough last season, and it figures to continue this season.

    Tight end

    It feels as if this might be the deepest and most talented group of tight ends in a long time. There are great players early and values late.

    Early rounds

    Brock Bowers, Raiders (ADP: 24.3): It didn't take long for new head coach Klint Kubiak to identify the top option in his offense.

    Middle rounds

    Colston Loveland, Bears (ADP: 45.0): Loveland's targets in the Bears' final four games last season: 10, 13, 10, 15.

    Harold Fannin Jr., Browns (ADP: 75.0): Fannin stood out when he shared time with David Njoku last season, and now Njoku is no longer there.

    Tucker Kraft, Packers (ADP: 88.8): He might not be full time until midseason, but even part-time Kraft is a threat.

    Later rounds

    Isaiah Likely, Giants (ADP: 127.4): Likely followed his head coach to the Giants in free agency so he can be the No. 1 tight end. There's no Mark Andrews around to block him.

    Terrance Ferguson, Rams (ADP: 165.6): Head coach Sean McVay has admired Ferguson's talents since the team drafted him in Round 2 last year.

    AJ Barner, Seahawks (ADP: 169.5): Those around the Seahawks have described Barner as an ascending player.

    Gunnar Helm, Titans (ADP: 170.6): Like many in the Titans' offense, poised to make a jump.

Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen led his position with 364.62 fantasy points last season, and for six consecutive years, he has finished among the game's top two scorers at quarterback. However, quarterback is a deep position in 2026.

One can make the case that nearly half the NFL teams have a QB worthy of starting for your fantasy team this season. Allen is awesome, but even last season he outscored vastly underrated Detroit Lions QB Jared Goff -- barely a top-10 performer at the position -- by only 67.56 points, or less than four points per week.

Allen also spent quite a bit of time handing the football off (or throwing) to RB James Cook III, fantasy's No. 6 scorer at the position last season. Cook turned his 342 touches into 1,912 scrimmage yards and 14 touchdowns, and for the second season in a row he was a notable bargain in terms of ESPN average draft position. This season, Cook isn't such a bargain, as he is going early in Round 2, but he remains worth it. He isn't alone among running backs.

In fact, this really is a year to invest a pick or two at running back early. If you don't, you might be quite disappointed in the options available later.

In relation to Allen and his relatively slight superiority over other quarterbacks, for example, this narrative does not exist at running back. Standard fantasy starting lineups require one QB and two RBs, but -- considering the flex position -- many can and will play three RBs. Cook outscored the No. 20 RB, Denver Broncos youngster RJ Harvey, by 95.6 points. He outscored Chicago Bears RB Kyle Monangai, 30th among RBs, by 155.5.

Fantasy managers cannot wait to build around running backs, so even if Cook, Baltimore Ravens star Derrick Henry, Omarion Hampton of the Los Angeles Chargers, Chase Brown of the Cincinnati Bengals and others aren't what we would call "value picks," they are very much in demand because running back is not deep, unlike quarterback. We covet volume running backs, and there simply aren't enough. This is the year to secure a few in the early rounds, led by Cook, Henry and Hampton.

As always, the annual "Do Draft" list focuses on players who keep ending up on my fantasy teams, either from valuable practice mock drafts or the ones that count, considering value versus standard ADP. I keep gravitating toward these players, either for strategic reasons -- such as waiting a long time to choose a QB or two -- or because the players make sense or seem undervalued. Cook might not be undervalued, since he has proved himself with 32 touchdowns and safe volume the past two seasons, but he is a player to build around because he is reliable. Allen is reliable as well, but the depth at quarterback and running back is hardly similar.

Henry, one of my annual favorites, has been heavily featured in this "Do Draft" space for years, and he followed up his excellent 2024 season of 1,921 rushing yards and 18 total touchdowns with 1,595 rushing yards and 16 scores. Henry boasts double-digit touchdowns for eight consecutive seasons, and a top-10 fantasy finish at running back in six of the past seven. He is 32, and although that brings legitimate concern, there is no indication of decline. Henry is neither overvalued nor undervalued this season. Like Cook, he is someone to target.

Every season I try many strategies of securing players, and how I feel about the results tends to direct how I approach the drafts that matter to me. This season, I covet a few volume running backs early even if that means ignoring my rankings of a WR with a late first-round pick. There is receiver depth. There is always quarterback depth.

Try out some mock drafts and see how you feel!

More at running back

  • Dallas Cowboys starter Javonte Williams might belong in the same ADP range as Brown after an outstanding 2025 season with 1,201 rushing yards and 13 total touchdowns. Williams likely would have finished as the No. 10 RB if he had played in a meaningless Week 18 game. The Cowboys boast an electric offense and are committed to his volume. More than a few (maybe almost all?) of the RBs going in Round 5 and later scare me. Williams might be in a tier by himself, or perhaps bumped up with the others.
  • New Houston Texans starter David Montgomery isn't necessarily safe or gleaming with upside, but he also doesn't cost you a high draft pick as he is going in Round 8. In the AFC for the first time, Montgomery begins the third chapter of an underrated career at age 29, and reasonable minds can debate what level of volume he will receive. Montgomery hasn't been a true featured back for years (through little fault of his own), but that doesn't mean he is incapable of a return to reliable RB2 range. The rushing yards and touchdowns should be there. This is a bargain player.
  • I am generally not targeting first-year players, but Seattle Seahawks rookie Jadarian Price enters a positive situation with the defending Super Bowl champions. Kenneth Walker III is gone, and the Seahawks never seemed particularly concerned about replacing him. Price couldn't pile on the stats at Notre Dame with Arizona Cardinals pick Jeremiyah Love there as well, and he might not play much on passing downs, but I see a bruiser with 200-plus rushing attempts and double-digit touchdowns coming. I see an RB2 option lurking, and in his ADP range I want little part of the RB timeshares with the New England Patriots, Pittsburgh Steelers, Carolina Panthers and Minnesota Vikings.
  • Kenny Gainwell boasts a strong chance of outscoring incumbent Bucky Irving with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and I will reach a few rounds to grab him.
  • I also will reach a bit for Broncos starter J.K. Dobbins. He might never appear in 17 games in a season, but perhaps this will be his first 1,000-yard rushing campaign. Harvey is the third-down back.
  • Washington Commanders newcomer Rachaad White will be a popular in-season flex option as he steamrolls toward 70 receptions. Former Commanders option Chris Rodriguez Jr. should join him; he catches few passes but can earn early-down volume and approach double-digit touchdowns in Jacksonville. I will take a chance on New Orleans Saints pass catcher Alvin Kamara in the late rounds, too.

Quarterback

  • San Francisco 49ers starter Brock Purdy is going outside the top 100 in ADP. He was the No. 6 QB fantasy scorer in 2023 with 4,280 passing yards and 31 touchdowns, and he was on a similar scoring pace last year. Perhaps we cannot assume 17 games or pristine health for his targets around him, but I see a borderline QB1 option going as a clear backup in many leagues.
  • Kansas City Chiefs star Patrick Mahomes (knee) is playing in Week 1 ... well, I believe he will. Don't expect the same rushing prowess as last season, but I would take the over on 4,000 passing yards and 30 TDs. How can one bet against Mahomes?
  • Lions starter Jared Goff is rostered in barely 50% of ESPN leagues and is going 16th at his position despite finishing as a top-10 QB fantasy scorer in each of the past four seasons. No, really, it's true. What production! What consistency! I stop short of ranking him in the top 10, but as I write this section I wonder, "Why would it be so silly to do so?" Perhaps, as with Cowboys RB Williams, I need to move Goff up a tier.
  • I continue to take chances (mainly in superflex formats) on new Vikings starter Kyler Murray and Saints sophomore Tyler Shough. I refuse to believe that the Miami Dolphins will be so embarrassingly bad on offense that new QB Malik Willis will fail, especially with his running ability.

Wide receiver

  • Vikings star Justin Jefferson might not reprise his 2024 numbers, but I bet he comes close. He doesn't need amazing QB play, he just needs competency there. Murray should be more than competent. Meanwhile, Vikings teammate Jordan Addison enters a critical season. His rookie numbers (70 receptions, 911 yards, 10 TDs) are in play, making Addison a bargain pick -- especially with an ADP below all of the Jacksonville Jaguars WRs fighting for targets.
  • Newly paid Ravens starter Zay Flowers finished seventh in WR scoring last season despite underwhelming QB play, yet he is 17th among WRs in ADP. No, I don't rank Flowers as a top-10 WR, but something doesn't make sense here. I am fine with Flowers and a pair of reliable RBs among my first three selections.
  • Lions starter Jameson Williams might never approach 100 receptions (75 is reasonable), so his value might be higher in non-PPR formats. Even so, his QB is durable and productive, the creative offense (usually) sings and Detroit's schedule this season might be the most favorable in the sport. This could be the TD breakout campaign. Williams easily boasts WR1 upside.
  • I admit I might be too generous to 49ers newcomer Mike Evans, but he surpassed 1,000 receiving yards and scored 11 touchdowns (No. 7 WR fantasy scorer) only two seasons ago, doing so in 14 games. I don't expect quite that, but something like a reliable WR2 season makes sense.
  • Indianapolis Colts starter Josh Downs is a wise breakout option after the team sent Michael Pittman Jr. to the Steelers. Downs enters his fourth season poised for his most targets, catches and, well ... everything. He and Alec Pierce are different. I like a healthy Pierce, but it seems he is not healthy (and Pittman over fellow Steeler DK Metcalf is a reasonable take, too).
  • I don't get the ordinary projections for new Tennessee Titans starter Wan'Dale Robinson. I do get that the Titans grabbed rookie Carnell Tate in the draft to be their new top WR, but that scenario doesn't always work out initially. Throw Robinson into the slot and everyone enjoys 80-plus catches, even if they're somewhat hollow. That's valuable in PPR.
  • Someone will catch passes in Miami. Relative fantasy afterthought Malik Washington can surprise.

Tight end

  • Nothing against the top options, but I still like to build with RBs and WRs. So, when thinking about TEs after Harold Fannin Jr. (whom I like) goes off the board, Packers breakout Tucker Kraft deserves a better ADP (perhaps in the Fannin neighborhood). Kraft is recovering well from the ACL tear, and it sure seems like he will play in Week 1. He is Green Bay's top receiving option.
  • The good news is the Ravens' Mark Andrews outlasted now-New York Giant Isaiah Likely and earned his own contract extension. Andrews was disappointing in 2025, but there are no excuses now: His volume must rise. Andrews has been a top-five fantasy TE in five of the past seven seasons. It is hardly outrageous to expect a return to the top 10, and if he starts slowly, streaming is an option at the position. I bet the Vikings' T.J. Hockenson, Bills' Dalton Kincaid and Patriots' Hunter Henry outproduce their lowly ADPs, too.

Now that everyone has played at least two preseason games and we are two weeks from the regular-season opener, it's a good time to ask ESPN NFL Nation reporters questions that fantasy managers have ahead of their drafts.

How are position battles shaping up? What are the prospects of players returning from injuries? Which rookies are in position to have an impact? Which players will bounce back in 2026?

Here's a look around the NFL with answers to the biggest fantasy questions.

Arizona Cardinals

What is your level of confidence that Marvin Harrison Jr. will outproduce Michael Wilson?

It's about 50-50. Harrison will be the first read on most passes, and QB Jacoby Brissett will look to him to make big plays. However, the two don't have a long rapport together because of Harrison's injuries last season. On the other hand, Brissett knows what Wilson can do. With TE Trey McBride also an established threat, Wilson, who should be a top target option after his 1,006 yards last season, might end up being the third read on some plays. -- Josh Weinfuss

Baltimore Ravens

After a big drop-off in rushing attempts in 2025, will Lamar Jackson get back to using his legs again this season?

Jackson likely won't average nine carries per game like he did from 2018 to 2023, but he should run more than he did last season. The two-time NFL MVP has impressed teammates with his scrambles during training camp. "I feel like he might have gotten faster somehow," safety Kyle Hamilton said. As far as designed quarterback runs, new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle said it will vary game by game depending on the matchup. -- Jamison Hensley

Buffalo Bills

No Bills player has had 825 receiving yards or six TDs since 2023. Will DJ Moore change that? 

As long as Moore stays healthy, this is within reach. The connection between Josh Allen and Moore has been on display. Other players will see the ball -- including TE Dalton Kincaid -- but it's ramping up to be a big season for Moore. "I'm going to go out and make an assumption that it's going to be awesome to do that every single game ... to get [Moore] the ball early and often," Allen said after the first preseason game. -- Alaina Getzenberg

Carolina Panthers

How do you expect the backfield touches to be split between Chuba Hubbard and Jonathon Brooks?

Given Hubbard's recent hamstring injury, the Panthers are likely to lean on Brooks a bit more frequently than expected to start the season. Brooks, who is coming off back-to-back ACL surgeries on his right knee, has looked dynamic as a pass catcher, and he could figure heavily in the third-down work while rotating with Hubbard on a drive-to-drive basis. -- Mike Kaye

Chicago Bears

What are your expectations for the three primary pass catchers: Luther Burden III, Colston Loveland and Rome Odunze? 

I expect there to be a different leading receiver most weeks for the Bears. That was the case in Ben Johnson's inaugural season when Loveland finished his rookie campaign No. 1 in receptions, yards and touchdowns. Chicago uses so many multiple-TE formations that Loveland will once again be among Caleb Williams' most targeted and productive weapons. Odunze (who appears back to form in camp) and Burden will put up numbers, but I would be surprised if there are multiple 1,000-yard receivers given the Bears' reliance on the run game and how much Johnson likes to spread the ball around. -- Courtney Cronin

Denver Broncos

Will any one player emerge as the primary threat in the Broncos' backfield?

Get ready to ask this question over and over as -- if things go the way Sean Payton wants -- the Broncos split the workload among J.K. Dobbins, Jonah Coleman and RJ Harvey. Consider that between the 2006 and 2021 seasons (excluding the 2012 season when Payton was suspended) Payton's Saints teams had a 200-carry back just five times. And in three previous seasons in Denver, he has had a 200-carry back just once, in 2023 when the roster wasn't yet built the way he wanted. The smart advice is to be ready for the Broncos to use a committee until your eyes tell you otherwise. -- Jeff Legwold

Green Bay Packers

Which wide receiver do you expect to emerge as the top producer this season?

That depends on how top producer is defined. If it's yards per catch, it will be Christian Watson because of his speed and downfield ability. If it's volume, it could be Matthew Golden. He did not get the kind of opportunities he had hoped for last season as a rookie and not only is he determined to make up for that, but the offense is better suited to do so given that Watson, Golden and Jayden Reed are the clear-cut top three receivers. Last season, the Packers tried to spread the ball around to five or six wideouts. -- Rob Demovsky

Houston Texans

Is veteran David Montgomery the clear leader in this backfield?

Montgomery told ESPN he believes Texans' offensive coordinator Nick Caley is going to use his full capability of running inside or outside and being a receiving threat. The Texans wanted him because he will add a physical presence to their rushing attack. That doesn't mean backup Woody Marks will vanish, though. Marks will be involved, but it'll be a 70-30 split between the two backs. -- DJ Bien-Aime

Indianapolis Colts

What are realistic expectations for Alec Pierce in his return from ankle surgery?

This is a dicey projection, given it's a lower-body injury to a speedy receiver. But Pierce can still impact the offense even if he isn't initially at 100%. His route running and ability to contribute on short and intermediate routes is underrated, and he'll be expected to expand his menu of routes now that he is the team's clear No. 1 receiver. Don't expect Pierce to be an afterthought in the offense upon his return. -- Stephen Holder

Jacksonville Jaguars

How will the backfield duo of Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. be used?

The Jaguars have been gradually increasing Rodriguez's workload as he returns from a foot injury. They both shared the workload in 11-on-11 in a joint practice against the Panthers. Tuten has more experience as a pass catcher (10 catches as a rookie in 2025 versus Rodriguez's six in three seasons with Washington) and might get more third-down work if LeQuint Allen's soft tissue injury extends into the regular season. -- Michael DiRocco

Kansas City Chiefs

Is it reasonable to expect Patrick Mahomes to put up his usual production as a passer this season?

Mahomes has looked exceptional in training camp, leading one to believe he can have a bounce-back season, especially with the help of running back Kenneth Walker III. Much of Mahomes' production will be in the hands -- quite literally -- of his receivers, a collection of players who have plenty to prove this season. Rookie Cyrus Allen has been impressive in camp. If any quarterback can uplift the trio of Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton, it's Mahomes. -- Nate Taylor

Los Angeles Chargers

How much different will this offense be with Mike McDaniel as playcaller, and who benefits most?

Quarterback Justin Herbert will get the ball out a lot quicker in this offense, giving pass catchers more opportunities to get the ball in space to create yards after the catch. There should also be a lot more screens and motions than when Greg Roman was calling plays. As for who should benefit most? Everyone. McDaniel is responsible for some of the most explosive offenses in league history. There's no reason to think that will stop this season. -- Kris Rhim

Los Angeles Rams

Will Blake Corum continue to get a bigger piece of the pie in the Rams' backfield and eat into Kyren Williams' numbers?

Yes, I expect Corum's usage to increase this season. Last season, Williams and Corum had close to a 65-35 split, and I could see that being closer to 50-50 this season. During training camp, Williams said Corum looks "a lot leaner" after the offseason. "He looks a lot more explosive," Williams said. -- Sarah Barshop

Miami Dolphins

Should Malik Willis be taken more seriously by fantasy managers, despite a lack of proven pass catchers?

As a bona fide starter? I don't think I'd go that far. Willis' floor will always be higher than the average streaming starter because of his rushing output -- whether it be from scrambling or designed runs. In his lone appearance of the preseason, he looked decisive throwing the ball as well, but he's more of a spot starter than a weekly contributor. The Dolphins play one of the most difficult schedules in the NFL this season, which bodes well for game flow but could prove difficult in terms of weekly matchups. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques

Minnesota Vikings

How will touches be split between Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason?

Throughout training camp, Jones has been on the field for the first snaps of work by the No. 1 offense. But it's important to note that Mason has rotated through during those reps, while other running backs have worked with the No. 2 and No. 3 teams: a visual snapshot of what is likely to happen in the regular season. Jones and Mason will rotate, with Jones likely getting more snaps but Mason potentially more carries. -- Kevin Seifert

New England Patriots

How will Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson be used?

Stevenson is the clear-cut No. 1 option, with the coaching staff having the highest level of confidence in his pass-protection skills. Henderson is the home run hitter to complement that. Injuries are always challenging to project, but if each player remains healthy over the course of the season, the projection here would be a 65-35 split in favor of Stevenson, with insurance in the form of an RB3 (who has yet to emerge in a multiplayer competition). -- Mike Reiss

New Orleans Saints

How much does Jordyn Tyson's injury affect the fantasy breakout talk around Tyler Shough?

Not much. Shough could be a boom-or-bust play this year, depending on how much he and the Saints' offense have grown since last season. Shough will likely rely heavily on players like WR Chris Olave and TE Juwan Johnson, so if you believe he's ready to take a big step forward, having Tyson out to start the season shouldn't make a difference. -- Katherine Terrell

New York Giants

How much does the signing of Najee Harris impact Cam Skattebo's role?

It probably doesn't affect Skattebo too much. He's still the Giants' top choice at RB. Harris seems more like Skattebo insurance than anything else. If he eats at anyone's workload, it's likely to be that of Tyrone Tracy Jr. and not Skattebo. -- Jordan Raanan

Philadelphia Eagles

Will rookie Makai Lemon be an impact player as the WR2?

Lemon has been sidelined with a hamstring injury for almost all of camp and missed minicamp this spring for the same reason, so he has had little time to build chemistry with Jalen Hurts. When healthy, he operated primarily as the starting slot receiver, getting plenty of catch-and-run opportunities. I'd temper expectations for the beginning of the season, with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks likely to command the most targets among receivers early. -- Tim McManus

Pittsburgh Steelers

What is the Steelers' plan for the backfield tandem of Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle?

Having two solid running backs to rotate is good news for the Steelers' offense but bad news for fantasy managers. Through training camp practices and the second preseason game, it seems that the two will split carries fairly evenly. Warren, the better pass catcher of the two, seems to be the third-down preference. In the second preseason game against the Jets, Warren played nine snaps to Dowdle's 10. Each finished with five carries, with Warren rushing for 17 yards and Dowdle getting 18. -- Brooke Pryor

San Francisco 49ers

What is the vibe from camp on George Kittle's return from Achilles surgery and on what De'Zhaun Stribling will contribute as a rookie?

Kittle came off the PUP list and returned to practice Sunday, which gives him a chance to be ready for Week 1, although traveling to (and playing in) Australia might be a bit ambitious. Stribling, meanwhile, looks like the rare rookie wideout ready to contribute early for coach Kyle Shanahan. He has played all of the receiver spots in camp, but the slot position seems like it might be his primary home for the time being. -- Nick Wagoner

Seattle Seahawks

What is the latest on Zach Charbonnet's potential return, and how do you expect that to affect Jadarian Price?

Charbonnet appears to be on track to return sooner than you might expect given that he had ACL surgery in February. Week 1 still feels unlikely, but sometime in the first half of the season hardly seems out of the question. Price will be the lead back in the meantime, with George Holani and Emanuel Wilson mixing in. Price might suffer early on from not playing in the preseason, but the Seahawks are playing the long game and sacrificing those reps to try to keep him healthy. -- Brady Henderson

Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Will Bucky Irving bounce back this season, or is this going to be a backfield committee?

Irving is still the guy, and the return to more of a wide zone run scheme like the team had in 2024 under Liam Coen should benefit him, along with improved health. In limited action in his second preseason game -- in which the starters played two series -- he had 14 yards on three rushes. Kenny Gainwell, meanwhile, saw one rushing attempt. In Gainwell, they have a third-down back and someone who can withstand contact should Irving get dinged up again. But I wouldn't shy away from Irving this year because of Gainwell's presence. Plus, they do have some "pony" packages where you'll see both on the field at the same time. -- Jenna Laine

Tennessee Titans

What is realistic to expect from rookie Carnell Tate statistically?

Tate will gradually work his way into the lead receiver role, but he will share a lot of targets with Wan'Dale Robinson, which will cut into Tate's reception total. It's reasonable to have Tate in the 70-80 reception range with 800-900 yards and six to eight touchdowns. Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll has shown he's willing to feature a rookie receiver (Malik Nabers), and QB Cam Ward has already shown a penchant for going to Tate in the red zone. -- Turron Davenport

Washington Commanders

How does the team plan to deploy Rachaad White and Jacory Croskey-Merritt?

That remains to be seen. However, Washington views Croskey-Merritt as a good fit in this offense -- with a lot of outside zone runs -- because of his one-cut ability and explosiveness that others here lack. The key for him will be how he handles catching passes out of the backfield, as it would allow the team to use him in a larger role. White is the Commanders' best pass-catching threat out of the backfield. If nothing else, he will handle that role. -- John Keim
