Now that everyone has played at least two preseason games and we are two weeks from the regular-season opener, it's a good time to ask ESPN NFL Nation reporters questions that fantasy managers have ahead of their drafts.

How are position battles shaping up? What are the prospects of players returning from injuries? Which rookies are in position to have an impact? Which players will bounce back in 2026?

Here's a look around the NFL with answers to the biggest fantasy questions.

Arizona Cardinals

What is your level of confidence that Marvin Harrison Jr. will outproduce Michael Wilson?

It's about 50-50. Harrison will be the first read on most passes, and QB Jacoby Brissett will look to him to make big plays. However, the two don't have a long rapport together because of Harrison's injuries last season. On the other hand, Brissett knows what Wilson can do. With TE Trey McBride also an established threat, Wilson, who should be a top target option after his 1,006 yards last season, might end up being the third read on some plays. -- Josh Weinfuss

Baltimore Ravens

After a big drop-off in rushing attempts in 2025, will Lamar Jackson get back to using his legs again this season?

Jackson likely won't average nine carries per game like he did from 2018 to 2023, but he should run more than he did last season. The two-time NFL MVP has impressed teammates with his scrambles during training camp. "I feel like he might have gotten faster somehow," safety Kyle Hamilton said. As far as designed quarterback runs, new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle said it will vary game by game depending on the matchup. -- Jamison Hensley

Buffalo Bills

No Bills player has had 825 receiving yards or six TDs since 2023. Will DJ Moore change that? 

As long as Moore stays healthy, this is within reach. The connection between Josh Allen and Moore has been on display. Other players will see the ball -- including TE Dalton Kincaid -- but it's ramping up to be a big season for Moore. "I'm going to go out and make an assumption that it's going to be awesome to do that every single game ... to get [Moore] the ball early and often," Allen said after the first preseason game. -- Alaina Getzenberg

Carolina Panthers

How do you expect the backfield touches to be split between Chuba Hubbard and Jonathon Brooks?

Given Hubbard's recent hamstring injury, the Panthers are likely to lean on Brooks a bit more frequently than expected to start the season. Brooks, who is coming off back-to-back ACL surgeries on his right knee, has looked dynamic as a pass catcher, and he could figure heavily in the third-down work while rotating with Hubbard on a drive-to-drive basis. -- Mike Kaye

Chicago Bears

What are your expectations for the three primary pass catchers: Luther Burden III, Colston Loveland and Rome Odunze? 

I expect there to be a different leading receiver most weeks for the Bears. That was the case in Ben Johnson's inaugural season when Loveland finished his rookie campaign No. 1 in receptions, yards and touchdowns. Chicago uses so many multiple-TE formations that Loveland will once again be among Caleb Williams' most targeted and productive weapons. Odunze (who appears back to form in camp) and Burden will put up numbers, but I would be surprised if there are multiple 1,000-yard receivers given the Bears' reliance on the run game and how much Johnson likes to spread the ball around. -- Courtney Cronin

Denver Broncos

Will any one player emerge as the primary threat in the Broncos' backfield?

Get ready to ask this question over and over as -- if things go the way Sean Payton wants -- the Broncos split the workload among J.K. Dobbins, Jonah Coleman and RJ Harvey. Consider that between the 2006 and 2021 seasons (excluding the 2012 season when Payton was suspended) Payton's Saints teams had a 200-carry back just five times. And in three previous seasons in Denver, he has had a 200-carry back just once, in 2023 when the roster wasn't yet built the way he wanted. The smart advice is to be ready for the Broncos to use a committee until your eyes tell you otherwise. -- Jeff Legwold

Green Bay Packers

Which wide receiver do you expect to emerge as the top producer this season?

That depends on how top producer is defined. If it's yards per catch, it will be Christian Watson because of his speed and downfield ability. If it's volume, it could be Matthew Golden. He did not get the kind of opportunities he had hoped for last season as a rookie and not only is he determined to make up for that, but the offense is better suited to do so given that Watson, Golden and Jayden Reed are the clear-cut top three receivers. Last season, the Packers tried to spread the ball around to five or six wideouts. -- Rob Demovsky

Houston Texans

Is veteran David Montgomery the clear leader in this backfield?

Montgomery told ESPN he believes Texans' offensive coordinator Nick Caley is going to use his full capability of running inside or outside and being a receiving threat. The Texans wanted him because he will add a physical presence to their rushing attack. That doesn't mean backup Woody Marks will vanish, though. Marks will be involved, but it'll be a 70-30 split between the two backs. -- DJ Bien-Aime

Indianapolis Colts

What are realistic expectations for Alec Pierce in his return from ankle surgery?

This is a dicey projection, given it's a lower-body injury to a speedy receiver. But Pierce can still impact the offense even if he isn't initially at 100%. His route running and ability to contribute on short and intermediate routes is underrated, and he'll be expected to expand his menu of routes now that he is the team's clear No. 1 receiver. Don't expect Pierce to be an afterthought in the offense upon his return. -- Stephen Holder

Jacksonville Jaguars

How will the backfield duo of Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. be used?

The Jaguars have been gradually increasing Rodriguez's workload as he returns from a foot injury. They both shared the workload in 11-on-11 in a joint practice against the Panthers. Tuten has more experience as a pass catcher (10 catches as a rookie in 2025 versus Rodriguez's six in three seasons with Washington) and might get more third-down work if LeQuint Allen's soft tissue injury extends into the regular season. -- Michael DiRocco

Kansas City Chiefs

Is it reasonable to expect Patrick Mahomes to put up his usual production as a passer this season?

Mahomes has looked exceptional in training camp, leading one to believe he can have a bounce-back season, especially with the help of running back Kenneth Walker III. Much of Mahomes' production will be in the hands -- quite literally -- of his receivers, a collection of players who have plenty to prove this season. Rookie Cyrus Allen has been impressive in camp. If any quarterback can uplift the trio of Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton, it's Mahomes. -- Nate Taylor

Los Angeles Chargers

How much different will this offense be with Mike McDaniel as playcaller, and who benefits most?

Quarterback Justin Herbert will get the ball out a lot quicker in this offense, giving pass catchers more opportunities to get the ball in space to create yards after the catch. There should also be a lot more screens and motions than when Greg Roman was calling plays. As for who should benefit most? Everyone. McDaniel is responsible for some of the most explosive offenses in league history. There's no reason to think that will stop this season. -- Kris Rhim

Los Angeles Rams

Will Blake Corum continue to get a bigger piece of the pie in the Rams' backfield and eat into Kyren Williams' numbers?

Yes, I expect Corum's usage to increase this season. Last season, Williams and Corum had close to a 65-35 split, and I could see that being closer to 50-50 this season. During training camp, Williams said Corum looks "a lot leaner" after the offseason. "He looks a lot more explosive," Williams said. -- Sarah Barshop

Miami Dolphins

Should Malik Willis be taken more seriously by fantasy managers, despite a lack of proven pass catchers?

As a bona fide starter? I don't think I'd go that far. Willis' floor will always be higher than the average streaming starter because of his rushing output -- whether it be from scrambling or designed runs. In his lone appearance of the preseason, he looked decisive throwing the ball as well, but he's more of a spot starter than a weekly contributor. The Dolphins play one of the most difficult schedules in the NFL this season, which bodes well for game flow but could prove difficult in terms of weekly matchups. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques

Minnesota Vikings

How will touches be split between Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason?

Throughout training camp, Jones has been on the field for the first snaps of work by the No. 1 offense. But it's important to note that Mason has rotated through during those reps, while other running backs have worked with the No. 2 and No. 3 teams: a visual snapshot of what is likely to happen in the regular season. Jones and Mason will rotate, with Jones likely getting more snaps but Mason potentially more carries. -- Kevin Seifert

New England Patriots

How will Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson be used?

Stevenson is the clear-cut No. 1 option, with the coaching staff having the highest level of confidence in his pass-protection skills. Henderson is the home run hitter to complement that. Injuries are always challenging to project, but if each player remains healthy over the course of the season, the projection here would be a 65-35 split in favor of Stevenson, with insurance in the form of an RB3 (who has yet to emerge in a multiplayer competition). -- Mike Reiss

New Orleans Saints

How much does Jordyn Tyson's injury affect the fantasy breakout talk around Tyler Shough?

Not much. Shough could be a boom-or-bust play this year, depending on how much he and the Saints' offense have grown since last season. Shough will likely rely heavily on players like WR Chris Olave and TE Juwan Johnson, so if you believe he's ready to take a big step forward, having Tyson out to start the season shouldn't make a difference. -- Katherine Terrell

New York Giants

How much does the signing of Najee Harris impact Cam Skattebo's role?

It probably doesn't affect Skattebo too much. He's still the Giants' top choice at RB. Harris seems more like Skattebo insurance than anything else. If he eats at anyone's workload, it's likely to be that of Tyrone Tracy Jr. and not Skattebo. -- Jordan Raanan

Philadelphia Eagles

Will rookie Makai Lemon be an impact player as the WR2?

Lemon has been sidelined with a hamstring injury for almost all of camp and missed minicamp this spring for the same reason, so he has had little time to build chemistry with Jalen Hurts. When healthy, he operated primarily as the starting slot receiver, getting plenty of catch-and-run opportunities. I'd temper expectations for the beginning of the season, with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks likely to command the most targets among receivers early. -- Tim McManus

Pittsburgh Steelers

What is the Steelers' plan for the backfield tandem of Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle?

Having two solid running backs to rotate is good news for the Steelers' offense but bad news for fantasy managers. Through training camp practices and the second preseason game, it seems that the two will split carries fairly evenly. Warren, the better pass catcher of the two, seems to be the third-down preference. In the second preseason game against the Jets, Warren played nine snaps to Dowdle's 10. Each finished with five carries, with Warren rushing for 17 yards and Dowdle getting 18. -- Brooke Pryor

San Francisco 49ers

What is the vibe from camp on George Kittle's return from Achilles surgery and on what De'Zhaun Stribling will contribute as a rookie?

Kittle came off the PUP list and returned to practice Sunday, which gives him a chance to be ready for Week 1, although traveling to (and playing in) Australia might be a bit ambitious. Stribling, meanwhile, looks like the rare rookie wideout ready to contribute early for coach Kyle Shanahan. He has played all of the receiver spots in camp, but the slot position seems like it might be his primary home for the time being. -- Nick Wagoner

Seattle Seahawks

What is the latest on Zach Charbonnet's potential return, and how do you expect that to affect Jadarian Price?

Charbonnet appears to be on track to return sooner than you might expect given that he had ACL surgery in February. Week 1 still feels unlikely, but sometime in the first half of the season hardly seems out of the question. Price will be the lead back in the meantime, with George Holani and Emanuel Wilson mixing in. Price might suffer early on from not playing in the preseason, but the Seahawks are playing the long game and sacrificing those reps to try to keep him healthy. -- Brady Henderson

Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Will Bucky Irving bounce back this season, or is this going to be a backfield committee?

Irving is still the guy, and the return to more of a wide zone run scheme like the team had in 2024 under Liam Coen should benefit him, along with improved health. In limited action in his second preseason game -- in which the starters played two series -- he had 14 yards on three rushes. Kenny Gainwell, meanwhile, saw one rushing attempt. In Gainwell, they have a third-down back and someone who can withstand contact should Irving get dinged up again. But I wouldn't shy away from Irving this year because of Gainwell's presence. Plus, they do have some "pony" packages where you'll see both on the field at the same time. -- Jenna Laine

Tennessee Titans

What is realistic to expect from rookie Carnell Tate statistically?

Tate will gradually work his way into the lead receiver role, but he will share a lot of targets with Wan'Dale Robinson, which will cut into Tate's reception total. It's reasonable to have Tate in the 70-80 reception range with 800-900 yards and six to eight touchdowns. Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll has shown he's willing to feature a rookie receiver (Malik Nabers), and QB Cam Ward has already shown a penchant for going to Tate in the red zone. -- Turron Davenport

Washington Commanders

How does the team plan to deploy Rachaad White and Jacory Croskey-Merritt?

That remains to be seen. However, Washington views Croskey-Merritt as a good fit in this offense -- with a lot of outside zone runs -- because of his one-cut ability and explosiveness that others here lack. The key for him will be how he handles catching passes out of the backfield, as it would allow the team to use him in a larger role. White is the Commanders' best pass-catching threat out of the backfield. If nothing else, he will handle that role. -- John Keim

Pithy quotes written in hot pink script. Video footage from late-night talk shows. Audio clips of live(ly) performances. The internet has attempted to celebrate Dolly Parton's memory with the volume and breadth befitting an icon.

Except there can never be enough for a person whose most adored trait was being too much. A living, breathing anomaly. Humble yet confident. Ambitious but kind. Petite and powerful. What made Dolly unique wasn't just that she did everything on her own terms and in her own way ... but that her unapologetic approach actually worked.

From shading Elvis to building an amusement park in the Smoky Mountains, Dolly's principles guided her business acumen. It's almost as if her conviction carried her career ... not the other way around.

Often in life, we spend so much time worrying about making the "right" decision that we forget why we're making it in the first place. For the intended result or for the enjoyment of the process? Ideally, both. Sometimes, the factors are so complex that decisions can't simply be influenced by fact. We gotta get into some feels.

We also have to acknowledge that we might whiff. Decision-making isn't a science. The algorithms and chatbots would like us to believe differently, suggesting (demanding?) that perfection is possible and efficiency is essential.

What they're missing is actual lived experience. A cellular understanding that the vector between choice and resolution does not, in fact, exist in a straight line. It's all swirly. Full of zigzags and beautifully jagged edges. Those spikes and slopes aren't just the data accrued but, also, lessons learned. Like Ms. Dolly said, "If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

Surrendering to fallibility makes room for ease. Viewing mistakes as opportunities -- rather than dead ends -- alters the trajectory of enjoyment. And all this relates to fantasy football.

For example, I could be totally wrong about Christian McCaffrey this year. Maybe he'll be the first running back in two decades to come off a 450-touch season (including the playoffs) and finish inside the top 10 fantasy producers at the position. The tomes of research I've uncovered suggest otherwise. That evidence hasn't stopped folks from screaming at the wind (and me). But my commitment to the facts in combination with my personal conviction keeps me from bending the knee.

It also keeps me smiling. Because there's satisfaction in standing 10 toes down when you've done the work. My fantasy team doesn't belong to the consensus. Yours shouldn't either. So draft with the confidence your squad deserves. Whether that's leaning into Christian Watson's volatility or eschewing Jakobi Meyers' floor, make this a signature season. And remember one more bit of wisdom from Dolly: "If you keep yourself out of the game for fear of losing, there is no way on this earth you're gonna win."

With that in mind, let's dig in for a closer look at the facts -- and feelings -- surrounding some of the biggest names in fantasy football this season.

 Lamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens

Coming off career-low rushing numbers, Jackson's redraft stock has plummeted. A deeper dive into the numbers reveals massive bounce-back appeal at an all-time discount. Jackson battled hamstring, toe, ankle and back injuries throughout the past season, missing four contests and playing through the pain for a handful of others. Before suffering the initial injury in Week 4, Jackson averaged 27.6 FPPG and was on pace for 30 passing scores. Even in a down effort, the Ravens QB averaged 18.1 FPPG in the games he was able to finish.

Jackson enters 2026 fully healthy and primed for a rebound. Backed by the NFL's fifth-easiest strength of schedule, Jackson's aerial appeal skyrockets with the addition of a rookie pass-catching quartet: wideouts Ja'Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt, alongside tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas. This influx of young talent meshes perfectly with new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle's aggressive, big-play philosophy. A conservative projection of just 120 rushing attempts still easily clears his path back to a top-five fantasy finish. Given the two-round gap between Josh Allen and Jackson, the Ravens QB is a strong value at his current ADP of right around 35.

 James Cook III, RB, Buffalo Bills

It wasn't Derrick Henry or Jonathan Taylor or Bijan Robinson who led the NFL in rushing yards last season. It was Cook. Amassing a career-high 1,612 rushing yards, Cook remained one of the slipperiest backs in the league, closing out the year as fantasy's RB5 in breakaway runs (16) and the RB7 in evaded tackles (77). Buoyed by an elite offensive line, the 26-year-old additionally managed 3.09 yards before contact (RB3, behind Jahmyr Gibbs and Blake Corum).

Ranking fourth at the position in scrimmage yards, Cook's ground numbers weren't the only stats to surge. The dual-threat talent also added 4.4 FPPG via receiving work. That's particularly noteworthy given new offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael's comments about getting Cook more involved in the passing game. Carmichael previously served as the New Orleans Saints' offensive coordinator when New Orleans selected Alvin Kamara in the third round of the 2017 NFL draft. Given Cook's projected volume, upside as a receiver and consistent weekly floor (only six games outside of the top 10 at the position in 2025), the Bills' RB1 is worthy of a first-round virtual selection.

 Bucky Irving, RB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Undersized but ultra-aggressive, Irving tore up the back half of his rookie campaign, becoming a premier fantasy asset in the process. Unfortunately, his high-impact approach took a physical toll, causing injuries that derailed the bulk of his second season. The Oregon product missed seven games due to a midfoot sprain and simultaneous shoulder dislocation suffered in Week 4 of 2025. The shoulder issue ultimately required offseason surgery, causing a recovery process that stretched into 2026. Even though Irving did not miss any preseason action specifically due to the shoulder, there remains hesitation about his ability to handle a robust workload.

Enter Kenny Gainwell. Tampa Bay let Rachaad White walk and replaced him with Gainwell, who is fresh off a career season in Pittsburgh. The RB4 in catches (73) and the RB5 in receiving yards (486), Gainwell posted the highest percentage of fantasy points via receptions (62%) in 2025. Given that 53% (RB5) of Irving's fantasy points were earned through the air and just 47% of his virtual production came from the rush, Irving's totals figure to recede. Factor in Sean Tucker's propensity for goal-line touchdown poaching and Bucky's 2026 profile appears increasingly bleak.

 Ladd McConkey, WR, Los Angeles Chargers

Who will be this year's JSN? It's a question I've been frequently asked over the spring and summer. While each season unfolds as its own unique expression and, therefore, such signature breakouts can't be guaranteed, identifying overlapping situations and players can be a useful exercise.

Much like Smith-Njigba, McConkey enters his third season boasting positional versatility and a history of being heavily targeted (over 100 looks in back-to-back efforts). While McConkey has done significant damage from the slot, his capacity to win across the formation aligns well with the arrival of new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. Just as Klint Kubiak expanded Smith-Njigba's route tree, McDaniel is primed to unlock a new tier of deployment for McConkey.

Anchored by Justin Herbert's deft arm talent and elevated by a swath of available targets -- inheriting the opportunities left behind by Keenan Allen, similar to the way JSN absorbed a void left by DK Metcalf -- McConkey stands at the precipice of a career-defining season. His underlying metrics prove he has the profile to capitalize on this workload, flashing exceptional efficiency and playmaking upside by averaging a stellar 2.79 yards per route run as a rookie. When stacked against the less-than-inspiring veteran wideouts typically available in the fifth round, McConkey's ceiling calls like a siren's song.

 Mike Evans, WR, San Francisco 49ers

Already skipping reps, Evans is a dicey proposition entering his age-33 season. Hamstring and collarbone issues sidelined the vet for nine games in 2025. A change of scenery does not appear to have provided relief, as he has battled calf, quad and groin injuries thus far into training camp. Even when he does suit up, the physical wear and tear on his body appears to have caught up with his production. Evans posted career lows in yards per route run (a 33.3% drop from 2024) and fantasy points per catch last season. The dip in efficiency capped the impact of his previously high-value grabs.

On the other hand, the red area of the field is exactly where Evans has thrived, ranking third of 77 qualified WRs in percentage of points scored via TD (38.8%) over the past three seasons. Combined with learning a new playbook and facing a bottom-10 strength of schedule, Evans faces an uphill battle to rebound in 2026.

 Rashid Shaheed, WR, Seattle Seahawks

Seattle re-signed Shaheed to a three-year, $51 million contract, signaling an increased role in the offense. The 27-year-old's previous experience in New Orleans indicates that he's up for the task. Shaheed averaged 11.6 FPPG alongside Chris Olave prior to being traded midseason. He also registered an impressive 22% target share (not much lower than Olave's 29% target share) from Weeks 1 through 9. Furthermore, Shaheed's 7.3 targets and 4.9 receptions per contest ranked 15th among wide receivers during that span.

Reports out of training camp suggest that the Seahawks plan to use Shaheed in the short-to-intermediate passing game, lifting the speedster's weekly floor above his usual deep-threat status. Because all other Seattle wide receivers -- outside of Smith-Njigba -- combined for a mere 82 catches, 1,100 yards and eight touchdowns last season, Shaheed has a massive opportunity to absorb that production and lock himself in as the team's clear-cut No. 2 WR. He is an absolute bull's-eye of a late-round dart throw in upcoming fantasy drafts.

 Colston Loveland, TE, Chicago Bears

No need to waste your energy debating between Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III for Bears pass catchers -- Loveland is the guy to roster. Equal parts reliable and dynamic, the No. 10 pick from a year ago figures draw a significant number of the 150 looks vacated due to the departures of Olamide Zaccheaus (65) and D.J. Moore (85). A sudden mover for his size (6-foot-6, 248 pounds), Loveland wins at the catch point and remains a threat after the catch. He averaged an impressive 1.96 yards per route run (TE6) as a 21-year-old rookie.

Unleashed by Ben Johnson down the stretch, the Michigan standout emerged as fantasy TE2 (behind only Trey McBride) from Weeks 9 through 18 of last year. He averaged a heart-stopping 12.0 targets, 7.0 catches and 94.5 receiving yards over his final four games (including the playoffs). There's little reason to believe he won't pick up where he left off. A staggering mismatch over the middle of the field, Loveland has the goods to finish as fantasy's No. 1 tight end this season. He's a prime target at the position in the fourth round of fantasy drafts.

As fantasy football draft season inches closer and closer, it's time for our annual predictions of sleepers, busts and breakout players. Interpretations of the terms can vary for each, but here are the definitions for our purposes:

• Sleeper: A player who is being overlooked and will outperform his average draft position (ADP) in 2026.
• Bust: A highly regarded player who will underperform in 2026, relative to his ADP/ranking.
• Breakout: A player who will put up career-best numbers in 2026 and make a huge impact.

Stephania Bell, Matt Bowen, Mike Clay, Tristan H. Cockcroft, Daniel Dopp, Tyler Fulghum, Eric Karabell, Liz Loza, Eric Moody and Field Yates each contributed a sleeper and a bust for the major offensive positions, as well as one breakout candidate. You can find their picks below, as well as their analysis and insights on a selection of players they felt most passionate about in each category.

Editor's note: This story will be updated throughout the preseason.

Jump to: Sleepers | Busts | Breakouts

Sleepers

Bell: Tyler Shough gave us a hint of things to come when he closed out his rookie season with six straight games of 17 or more fantasy points. He now adds a year of experience plus a new weapon to boost offensive production in pass-catching running back Travis Etienne Jr. Unfortunately, he'll have to wait to see if a second newcomer -- rookie WR Jordyn Tyson (hamstring, out until at least October) -- will serve as a solid complement to veteran fantasy star (yet oft-injured) Chris Olave. Like all fantasy-desirable quarterbacks, Shough adds value with his legs. Among all quarterbacks with at least 10 carries in 2025, Shough ranked second in percentage of carries (22.2%) from inside the 10-yard line, hinting at increased scoring opportunity.

Bowen: C.J. Stroud needs a running game -- and much more favorable third-down situations -- to play at a level comparable to his rookie season of 2023 (18.4 fantasy PPG). Houston upgraded the offensive line this offseason and traded for running back David Montgomery, critical pieces to creating more offensive tempo and rhythm with Stroud, who has the targets on the perimeter, led by Nico Collins, to throw with accuracy and produce explosive plays in the pass game. Stroud should be targeted in 2QB/superflex formats, and I expect him to post some QB1 weeks this season.

Dopp: Kenyon Sadiq. He's a rookie. On a bad organization. In a low-scoring offense. That doesn't have an elite QB. Oh, sorry, I was talking about what we said about Brock Bowers when he was coming into the league. We've seen premier rookie tight ends translate much faster to the fantasy game than our grandpappies did at our age. Sadiq is next in line and will see more of a hybrid WR/TE role. I love his low-cost, late-round value.

Loza: Suffering two ACL tears in the same knee within a span of 13 months certainly is reason for pause. Still, with an ADP 125.4, there's no denying Jonathon Brooks' sleeper appeal. Cleared for offseason team activities, the former Texas Longhorns standout is being eased into OTAs while receiving praise from Dave Canales about his return to health and explosive three-down skill set. After letting Rico Dowdle walk and ignoring the position during the NFL draft, Carolina appears confident in the 23-year-old's recovery. The first running back selected in 2024 (46th overall), Brooks is on the precipice of authoring a bust-to-boom comeback story for himself -- and fantasy managers.

Moody: Kenny Gainwell's role could be larger than expected in Tampa Bay. From Week 8 on last season, Gainwell, then a member of the Pittsburgh Steelers, averaged 13.3 touches and 17.8 fantasy points per game. He was also a capable receiver out of the backfield, ranking near the top of the position in yards per route run during that stretch. Rachaad White is gone, and Bucky Irving is projected for 61% of the touches for the Buccaneers, leaving Gainwell with standalone appeal and RB2 upside if his role grows.

Yates: I expect significant growth from QB Cam Ward in his second season functioning in an offense that will be improved. What the Titans lacked last year was a go-to target in the passing game (Elic Ayomanor led the team with a mere 89 targets in 2025), and Carnell Tate provides them with that (Wan'Dale Robinson will vacuum up a hefty share of targets too). Tate was the most pro-ready prospect in the 2026 NFL draft with his pristine route running and strong hands. I'm bullish.

Busts

Clay: Mike Evans is a future Hall of Famer, but he'll be hard-pressed to deliver a strong bounce-back campaign entering his age-33 season and first with the 49ers. Evans missed nine games due to injury last season and, even when active, his numbers were down (career low 12.1 PPG and one top-20 outing in seven full games). Over the past decade, Larry Fitzgerald and Julian Edelman are the only 33-plus-year-old wideouts to deliver top-25 fantasy campaigns, and they primarily worked in the slot and/or short range. Evans has generally made his hay as a downfield, red-zone playmaker. He'll benefit from Kyle Shanahan's efficient offense, but Evans panning out as your WR2/3 is going to require some serious touchdown fortune.

Cockcroft: Nothing against Harold Fannin Jr. as a player -- I see an excellent career ahead for him -- but I typically go against the crowd at tight end. Fannin had just about the best numbers anyone could've possibly expected from him in Cleveland last year, and the departure of David Njoku will surely heighten his draft-day price. Defenses will be more prepared for him this season, the Browns' quarterback situation remains a mess, and it's worth pointing out that Fannin has put in suspiciously little practice time throughout the offseason process. It's difficult to envision him exceeding his 2025 fantasy points total, but his ADP says that people think he will.

Dopp: Christian McCaffrey proved doubters wrong last year, reclaiming his position as a top-three fantasy running back. But this year is not last year. This year, McCaffrey is coming off a 450-touch season across the regular season and playoffs. Just like I did following Saquon Barkley's massive workload the year before, I'm fading the player with that kind of touch count in the previous season.

Fulghum: I hate to say it as a staunch Rams fan, but Matthew Stafford is screaming regression for 2026. His 2025 MVP campaign was magical. At age 38, Stafford started all 17 games, led the league in passing yards (4,707) and set career highs in passing TDs (46) and TD% (7.7). It is extraordinarily likely that most, if not all, of those numbers take a dip in 2026. Even if he plays all 17 games again -- which at his age is also going to be hard to do -- it's going to be tough to match what he did in 2025. He also adds next to nothing with his legs. This year we're drafting Stafford as QB9, when in 2025 his price tag was QB20! I hate to admit this, but Stafford is likely going to disappoint fantasy managers who invest in him this season.

Karabell: Malik Nabers is a terrific player, obviously, but the concern here is the right knee he tore in Week 4 of last season and the follow-up procedure from the spring. The Giants must be cautious with this young talent, and they appeared to plan ahead for the inevitability of Nabers starting this season late with their offseason acquisitions. Could Nabers overcome this and dominate for four-plus months like he did during his rookie season? He could, but there are far safer receiver options in the first two rounds. Invest in healthier players.

Moody: Josh Jacobs carries risk, as the warning signs are starting to stack up. He's 28 years old with 2,109 career touches, and there is also some uncertainty hanging over him as he deals with several off-field legal issues. On the field, his efficiency slipped last season, with his yards per carry dropping to 4.0. Jacobs also faded following a left knee injury and knee contusion last season, going from 21.1 touches and 19.6 fantasy points per game in his first nine games to 14.6 touches and 11.3 FPPG over his final five.

Breakouts

Bell: Omarion Hampton's strong-dual threat performance early in his rookie season (RB3 in Week 3 with 24.9 FP) had fantasy managers asking, "What if?" at season's end. What if he hadn't fractured his ankle and missed seven games? What if he had a full slate of games behind a healthy offensive line? Answers to those questions, along with "What can he do in a Mike McDaniel-led offense?" should be answered in 2026. Hampton's power and efficiency will enhance his production in this revamped Chargers offense, and if all relevant parties stay healthy, he could deliver on the RB1 promise he teased last year.

Bowen: With Mike Evans now in San Francisco, the door is open for Emeka Egbuka to emerge as the top target in Tampa Bay's offense. A detailed route runner who can create his own separation at all three levels of the field, Egbuka had four games of 20 or more fantasy points as a rookie, finishing with 68 receptions for 938 yards and six touchdowns. With the aggressive throwing mentality of Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield, don't be surprised if Egbuka finishes as a top-10 wide receiver in 2026.

Clay: Jeremiyah Love was selected third overall in April's draft, and recent history suggests that is a data point we can't ignore. Each of the past nine running backs drafted in the top 12 went on to finish top 12 in fantasy points at the position as a rookie. The nine backs averaged 289.1 touches, 1,456 scrimmage yards, 9.0 TDs and 17.3 fantasy PPG (that would have ranked seventh among RBs in 2025). Love has elite speed, a three-down skill set and was extremely efficient at Notre Dame. Expect a big workload and huge fantasy production right out of the gate.

Cockcroft: Travis Etienne Jr.'s departure from Jacksonville might have been met with some raised eyebrows, but I agree with the Jaguars on Bhayshul Tuten's upside and ability to deliver similar production in a starting role. As a rookie, Tuten turned seven of his 93 total touches into touchdowns and had the second-best missed tackles forced rate among running backs (31%), all that on the heels of standout 2024 at Virginia Tech as well as a combine in which he displayed his elite speed. Tuten's path to breaking through as a high-end fantasy RB2 is entirely clear.

Fulghum: Luther Burden III's second season in Chicago sets up nicely for him to break out in a BIG way. Ben Johnson calling plays. Caleb Williams at the trigger. DJ Moore and Olamide Zaccheaus out the door, leaving 150 vacated targets from last year. Rome Odunze's altered bone structure in his foot being his "new normal." All these factors form a tantalizing opportunity for Burden to bust out. He already showed on tape as a rookie that he is elite with the ball in his hands. His underlying efficiency metrics (albeit on a small sample), rank among some of the best all-time as a rookie. Had he reached qualifying thresholds, he would have ranked third among all WRs in yard per route run (2.92), behind only Puka Nacua and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Other rookies to post a YPRR north of 2.5 in the last decade include Nacua, Ja'Marr Chase, Justin Jefferson, A.J. Brown and Odell Beckham Jr. That is the bull ceiling case for Burden: a top-5 player at his position currently going as WR28 in ESPN drafts.

Karabell: The Seattle Seahawks moved on from Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III and drafted Jadarian Price, who didn't produce snazzy college numbers because he was Notre Dame's backup to the highly touted Jeremiyah Love, now with the Arizona Cardinals. Price did average 6.0 yards per carry and scored 13 touchdowns from scrimmage despite limited volume last season. Now, look at the Seahawks versus the Cardinals. Which situation is better? One can make the case that Price, with the Super Bowl champions and with less competition for backfield touches, is in a better situation. Love should be great, but he doesn't appear to be a bargain in ESPN ADP. Price is a terrific bargain, going five rounds later.

Yates: One can make the case that this is grabbing the low-hanging fruit, as Ashton Jeanty was a first-round pick in fantasy drafts last year and had a solid but unspectacular season. But the best moments from Jeanty -- his 31.8-point outing vs. the Texans in Week 16 comes to mind -- were a testament to his natural ability. The Raiders' offensive personnel, system and coaching should be dramatically improved this season, and Jeanty will benefit. Among players with at least 70 carries last season, Jeanty averaged 1.26 yards before contact per carry, dead last among those 80 players. It's a way better infrastructure for him all around.
